sentences.text: The name Ichthyotitan combines the Greek word for fish with a suffix meaning giant, echoing the earlier name Ichthyosaurus, which means 'fish lizard'.
The species name severnensis refers to the nearby Severn Estuary, the location near where the fossils were found.
Ichthyotitan exhibits a unique condition among ichthyosaurs where the surangular and angular bones, which are parts of the jaw, may have been fused in life.
Ichthyotitan is the only known shastasaurid from the Rhaetian, appearing 13 million years after its relatives.
Ichthyotitan is estimated to have reached nearly 25 meters in length, making it the largest known marine reptile.
Using Shastasaurus sikanniensis as a model, researchers estimated Ichthyotitan to be nearly the size of a blue whale.
The genus Ichthyotitan contains only one known species, I. severnensis, which was formally described as a new genus and species in 2024 by Lomax et al.
Ichthyotitan is known from two fragmentary lower jaw bones discovered in 2016 and 2020.
The holotype specimen of Ichthyotitan was found near Blue Anchor in Somerset within the Westbury Formation.
The first fragment of the holotype was discovered on May 28, 2020, by 11-year-old Ruby Reynolds and her father Justin Reynolds, with further expeditions until 2022 revealing additional pieces.

Ichthyotitan was likely an active predator that hunted smaller prey, including other marine reptiles, in an orca-like manner, though evidence of scavenging on Ichthyotitan fossils before burial explains the scarcity of known remains.
Histological characteristics suggest the holotype specimen was still growing, indicating it was a subadult or young adult.
Ichthyotitan is classified as a shastasaurid, extending the known range of this family to the latest Triassic, and belongs to the parent group Shastasauridae.
Ichthyotitan is classified within the class Reptilia.
Ichthyotitan lived during the Late Triassic, approximately 205 to 202 million years ago, in Somerset, United Kingdom, specifically during the Rhaetian stage from 205.7 to 201.4 million years ago.

The unique morphology of the posterior jaw in the Cuers specimen has been debated but is now linked to Ichthyotitan, while it is also debated whether shastasaurids were suction-feeders, as current research suggests their jaw structure does not fit that profile.
